https://nineoclock.ro/kpmg-pharma-and-he.text: ABOUT US NINE O’CLOCK STAFF 2024 COMMERCIAL OFFER – 2026 Subscribe to the Nine O’Clock 2026 CONTACT Special price offer 2026 with a 50% discount KPMG: Pharma and Healthcare – Why Resilience Has Become the Industry’s New Competitive Advantage Artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, regulatory pressure, employee expectations and data-driven decision-making are transforming the pharmaceutical and healthcare sectors on multiple fronts. Businesses are operating in a world where technological, regulatory and operational challenges intersect like never before, and innovation alone is no longer enough. These topics were explored during KPMG in Romania’s conference Pharma, Healthcare & Life Sciences Transformation – Business, Tax and Legal Insights , held in Bucharest on 28 July 2026. The event was moderated by Teodora Alecu, Director, Transfer Pricing and Head of Healthcare Sector services at KPMG in Romania, and Ioana-Zenaida Rizea-Popp, Partner, Audit and Co-Head of Healthcare Sector services. Edward Davies, CEE Life Sciences Lead, as well as KPMG specialists and industry leaders, also took part in the event, which examined the trends reshaping the sector, from artificial intelligence and cybersecurity to workforce transformation, predictive analytics, tax developments and compliance. The key message emerging from the conference was clear: the businesses which will thrive in the years ahead are those able to combine innovation with trust, strong governance and operational resilience. Resilience Is No Longer Optional The pharmaceutical and healthcare sectors are entering a new stage of transformation. While innovation remains a growth driver, companies are facing a growing number of challenges, from technological disruption and cyber risks to regulatory complexity and rising expectations from patients, employees and authorities. As a result, resilience is becoming a strategic differentiator rather than a defensive capability. This broader shift was reflected throughout the discussions at KPMG in Romania’s event. Edward Davies, CEE Life Sciences Lead, highlighted the strategic opportunity for Central and Eastern Europe to strengthen its role within Europe’s trusted Life Sciences networks. Clinical research, manufacturing, regulatory execution and digital capabilities are increasingly positioning the region as an important contributor to the future of the sector. According to Davies, trust, compliance and operational resilience are becoming strategic assets alongside scientific innovation. The trend is also reflected in market developments. Romania’s pharmaceuticals market continues to expand, and is now worth approximately RON 37.7 billion. At the same time, declining market volumes are increasing pressure on companies to improve efficiency, forecasting and resource allocation. Artificial Intelligence Is Moving From Experimentation to Reality Artificial intelligence emerged as one of the most significant themes of the event, reflecting the industry’s rapid transition from pilot projects to practical implementation. According to Eurostat, 20% of EU enterprises with at least 10 employees used AI technologies in 2025 [1] , compared with 13.5% in 2024 [2] , while adoption among large enterprises was 55% [3] . As AI moves from experimentation into core business processes, companies increasingly need secure and integrated environments where data, technology, controls and human oversight can work together effectively. Companies in the sector are increasingly exploring how AI can automate processes, improve productivity and support more informed decision-making. The conversation around AI focused on a clear shift taking place across industries: Companies in the sector are moving from experimentation to real-world implementation. Ileana Ionescu, Director, and Inga Țîgai, CEE Head of Tax & Legal Technology, explored how AI is already transforming business processes, including tax and compliance activities. Their message was clear: Technology alone is not enough. Long-term success depends on reliable data, strong governance and employees who are ready to work alongside new technologies. The audience also saw practical examples of AI in action, including a solution capable of extracting and processing invoice data for further registration and analysis. Another highlight was KPMG Digital Gateway, a centralized platform designed to simplify the management of tax obligations and processes, while providing access to analytics, reporting tools, industry insights and specialized expertise across the KPMG network. AI is no longer confined to back-office functions. Increasingly, it is finding its way into products and services that directly support patient care. Speaking from an industry perspective, Vadim Fântânari, Chief AI Officer at RebelDot and Co-Founder of WakeZ, discussed the growing role of AI-enabled healthcare solutions and presented WakeZ’s medical device, currently undergoing registration with the National Agency of Medicines. Developed to support people experiencing depression, the solution illustrates how artificial intelligence is beginning to reshape areas traditionally associated with clinical care and treatment support. However, innovation must go hand in hand with accountability. Dragoș Cherciu, Lawyer at KPMG Legal – Toncescu și Asociații, highlighted the need for clear governance structures and effective risk management as companies in the sector expand the use of AI in highly regulated environments. A similar trend is evident in the regulatory and transfer pricing landscape. Alexandra Ion, Associate Director, Transfer Pricing, explained that tax authorities are increasingly relying on digital tools, advanced analytics, and data-driven risk assessment methodologies, particularly in the area of transfer pricing. As a result, companies are expected to maintain robust documentation, ensure consistency across data sources, and be prepared to support their transfer pricing positions through greater transparency and timely access to information. This evolution is making compliance processes more data-driven and reinforcing the importance of preparedness in interactions with regulators. Trust and Compliance Are Becoming Strategic Assets Another major takeaway from the event was that compliance can no longer be treated as a box-ticking exercise. Across tax, legal and healthcare regulations, authorities are increasingly relying on technology, analytics and digital tools. As a result, companies in the sector are expected not only to comply with rules but also to demonstrate compliance through evidence, documentation and effective internal controls. This is particularly relevant for interactions between pharmaceutical companies and healthcare professionals, as well as transfer pricing matters. The growing digitalization of tax administration processes facilitates a more stringent approach to enforcing compliance. In a more regulated environment, trust is becoming a business asset. Organizations that can demonstrate transparency, accountability and strong governance are likely to be better positioned to withstand scrutiny and maintain stakeholder confidence. Risk, Resilience and Long-Term Performance As companies become more digital and interconnected, resilience is increasingly shaped by their ability to manage risk across multiple fronts. Cybersecurity, workforce transformation, data-driven decision-making and regulatory compliance are no longer separate priorities, but interconnected elements of long-term business performance. Gheorghe Vlad, Director, Cyber Security, emphasized that cybersecurity must be viewed as a business issue rather than a purely technical one. In the pharmaceutical and healthcare sectors, cyber incidents can disrupt manufacturing operations, affect supply chains and ultimately have an impact on patient access to treatment. As a result, cyber resilience is becoming a boardroom priority, with companies placing greater focus on business continuity and operational preparedness. People remain at the center of this transformation. Claudia Stan, Associate Director, People Services, discussed the implications of the European Pay Transparency Directive and the evolving expectations of today’s workforce. Transparency, equitable pay practices and trust are increasingly seen as essential factors in attracting, motivating and retaining talent in a competitive labor market. At the same time, organizations are turning to forecasting and predictive analytics to strengthen decision-making in an increasingly uncertain environment. Flavia Matei, Director, Strategy & Performance, highlighted how advanced analytics can help business leaders anticipate change, improve planning and make more informed strategic decisions. Laura Grădinescu, Lawyer, Managing Associate at KPMG Legal – Toncescu și Asociații, emphasized that companies must be able to demonstrate compliance through evidence, robust documentation and effective internal controls. Completing the legal perspective, Alex Slujitoru, lawyer, Partner at KPMG Legal – Toncescu și Asociații, examined current dispute trends affecting the pharmaceutical sector and highlighted the importance of identifying and addressing risks before they evolve into larger legal or operational challenges. Looking Ahead If there was one message that connected all discussions at the event, it was that the healthcare and life sciences sectors are facing a level of transformation unlike anything seen in recent years. From AI-powered innovation and cybersecurity risks to employee expectations, compliance demands and growing regulatory scrutiny, companies in the sector are being challenged to rethink how they operate, grow and create value. In this environment, success will increasingly belong to those that can manage complexity without slowing innovation, turn data into better decisions and build lasting trust with patients, employees, regulators and society at large. The future of healthcare will not be defined by technology alone. It will be defined by how effectively companies in the sector combine innovation, responsibility and resilience.
